name: Facet
text:
**Decision:** Use a **single, fixed dark theme** with a deep indigo base and a single, high-contrast accent color (e.g., electric blue) for all interactive elements.

This ensures **consistent visibility**—no eye strain from shifting contrasts—and **speeds up recognition** since users learn one palette. The trade-off is **less flexibility** for users who prefer light themes, but dark themes align with our competitive analysis (Manus, Graphify) and reduce cognitive load in low-light environments.

name: Pane
text: Fixed dark themes fail in mixed-lighting rooms—glare from screens or windows can wash out the indigo base, making the electric blue accent harder to spot than a lighter theme would. A better alternative is an auto-adjusting theme with a hard ceiling on brightness, capped at 60% contrast to prevent glare while keeping the deep base. Settle this by testing both in a bright, sunlit room with users who have light sensitivity—if the fixed theme forces squinting, the adjustable one wins.

name: Facet
text:
**Decision:** Use a **dynamic dark theme** that auto-adjusts brightness based on ambient light, but caps at 60% contrast to prevent glare. This keeps the deep indigo base for consistency while ensuring visibility in mixed-lighting rooms. The trade-off is slightly slower load times for the brightness sensor to kick in, but it guarantees the interface remains usable in any environment.

name: Pane
text: Auto-adjusting themes add complexity users won’t tolerate—brightness sensors fail in 20% of real rooms, and the 60% cap still risks washing out the indigo in bright daylight. A better alternative: a **light theme with a dark sidebar**—the sidebar holds the interactive elements in deep indigo, while the main view uses a soft gray background to reduce glare; settle it by testing both in a mixed-lighting room with 10 users—if the sidebar’s contrast holds up under phone flashlights, it wins.
